title: Altair Aether
note: Our own design: a ~300 kg lunar communications relay, fired off a mass driver near the lunar south pole into a 700 km circular polar orbit, one plane of a constellation, built from real flight hardware where it exists. Frame: x along the track (the direction of travel, and the craft's axis: the launch load runs down it), z up, y left. The craft's separation plane is at x = 0; the sled and the rails are behind and below it. Pass 1: structure, tank, main thruster, sled and rails. Pass 2: propulsion (eight 1 N thrusters, latch valve, fill and drain valves, lines). Pass 3: power (two solar wings, deployed; two batteries). Pass 4: comms, resized for the constellation (two K-band user tiles and an S-band antenna on the Moon-facing top, a K-band Earth tile and the X-band array on the bottom, laser terminals ahead and behind, transponder). Pass 5: attitude (four reaction wheels, two star trackers, sun sensors, IMU). Pass 6: electronics (power control unit, power cables; a reserved slot for the flight computer and valve drivers, which are designed separately). Pass 7: thermal (silvered-Teflon radiators on five sides, a blanket on the Moon-facing top, heaters). Pass 8: deployment (wings folded on hinges for the launch, hold-downs; click a wing to unfold).

orbit_altitude.quote: The left limit i_min shows little variation with the altitude, around values 55° < i_min < 60°, while the right limit i_max increases with the altitude, reaching i_max = 90° at about the altitude a − rL = 1300 km.
orbit_altitude.note: km, circular and polar (decided 2026-11-04). The paper's Figure 5 (GRAIL field to degree 10, Earth and Sun; runs of 10 to 14 years) shows circular polar orbits at 300, 500, 700 and 900 km lasting the whole run; at 2000 and 3000 km they fall in. 700 km keeps clear of both ends: the lunar field dominates below about 500 km (folta_2008), the Earth's pull destabilises polar orbits from about 1300 km.

also.quote: Lunar Gravity (potential) is major perturbation below 500km altitude
At 200 km altitude, impact is avoided as the altitude variations are bounded.

constellation.value: many small craft on low circular polar orbits, the planes spread by launching through the month as the Moon turns under the track
constellation.quote: the ad-hoc Lunar constellation consists of 98 low-altitude satellites, evenly distributed across seven circular polar orbital planes, alongside two satellites in a frozen orbit at an altitude of 5,500 km
constellation.note: NASA's study flies at 100 km, which it calls unstable ("operating for fewer than 90 days" without maintenance); ours flies at 700 km (orbit_altitude)

open_questions: Orbit (decided 2026-11-04): circular and polar at 700 km (orbit_altitude). legnaro_2024's lifetime maps start from one set of angles (ω0 = Ω0 = 0) and sample 300, 500, 700, 900, 2000 and 3000 km; where between 900 and 1300 km polar orbits stop surviving isn't pinned down, and 700 km stays clear of it. The altitude still swings over the years (nasa_lro_sk's 200 km run: about 130 to 270 km), so keeping the craft evenly spaced in a plane needs small burns.

Constellation: the craft now carries a node's comms (user tiles, laser links ahead and behind, an Earth tile), but how many craft per plane and how many planes isn't designed; no published study sizes one at 700 km. Laser links to the neighbouring planes aren't fitted: their place would be the upper slanted sides, where the wings fold for the launch. The SCOT30 is due 'TRL 8 by Q1/2028'.
Run-out past the map: at 1.815 km/s the shot stays within about 1 km of the 1737.4 km sphere for some 155 km; beyond the 87S map's edge (68 km past the track) it needs a wider elevation map to check.
Propulsion has no filter or pressure transducer yet (no sourced part found); the thruster layout is our own, not copied from a flown craft.

Comms: no maker publishes a flat array for LunaNet's proximity K-band, so the user tiles are sized as Boeing's 25.5-27.0 GHz tile (user_array), shown by NASA as a future product; the S-band antenna's size is estimated and its 70° beam falls short of the footprint's edge; the EnduroSat X-band array's band (8025-8400 MHz) sits below the 8450-8500 MHz lunar band; no low-gain antenna toward the Earth for safe mode beyond it.
Attitude: the wheel pyramid's tilt and the sensors' places are our own; coverage of the two coarse sun sensors is not a full sphere (safe mode would also lean on the fine sensor and the trackers).

Electronics: the Starbuck-Mini is rated 20 kRAD and '5–7 years in LEO'; whether that covers five years in lunar orbit (no Van Allen belts to cross, since it launches from the Moon, but solar particle events) isn't checked. Its bus follows the battery (22-34 V), not a regulated 28 V. The flight computer and valve drivers come from the separate design; the power budget waits for them.

Thermal: sized by hand for the worst cold-side case (600 W, no sun); not checked against the hot case at periselene (the sunlit Moon's infrared on the radiators) or the 2 h shadow (heater power). Lines and valves need heaters too (not modelled).

Deployment: the wings are shown folded for the launch (click a wing to unfold it); the hold-downs are placeholders, the panels' hinge hardware isn't modelled, and the wing drive's size is still an estimate.
